*Overview of section 7, version 0.2, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author's own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. Companion to the Climate Fiscal AI Tools. Version 0.1 (September 2026) is in `7.0.Overview/8.PreviousVersions`.*

# The standard: a ministry must be able to check it {.unnumbered}

A diagnostic a ministry cannot check is a recommendation it must take on trust, and recommendations taken on trust do not survive the first official who disagrees with them. The tools in this section are therefore built to a reproducibility standard rather than to analytical sophistication. Every intermediate step is visible. Defaults can be defended line by line. Where an AI model drafts a stage, it does so under a written specification and every line is checked against the source text or data.

Each tool answers a question a ministry already asks, from data it already has. None needs a new survey or a model run by another institution. The worked examples in the papers use public data, the tools' own country results labelled as illustrative, or clearly labelled stylized numbers.

# Read the excise system against its externalities (paper 7.1) {.unnumbered}

Excise schedules grow line by line until nobody can read them whole. The Excise-Fiscal Diagnostic sorts every line into a small typology, maps it onto 30 standard lines and scales each rate three ways: US dollars per standard physical unit, share of the consumer price, and implied revenue as a share of GDP. It then sets fuel rates against a corrective benchmark built from one fixed set of values for carbon, air pollution, accidents, congestion and road damage, and health excises against published health benchmarks. Run on the 2026 excise law of Sierra Leone and Liberia, it finds excise revenue of 1.25–1.28 and 0.37 percent of GDP, against an African average of 2.4. Sierra Leone draws about nine-tenths of its excise from fuel, taxed at USD 0.23 per liter of petrol on a large base. Liberia taxes fuel only through levies of USD 0.095 per liter, below the cost of carbon alone at USD 50 a tonne, taxes spirits at less than half the beer rate per liter of alcohol, and books no excise on imported tobacco (illustrative results from the diagnostic, not official estimates). In the paper's stylized country, diesel is taxed at less than half its corrective rate, and its largest unpriced cost is air pollution rather than carbon.

# Link energy investment to growth, revenue and debt (paper 6.5, section 6) {.unnumbered}

The Macro-Fiscal-Energy Scenario Tool chains a model of mitigation investment needs, a carbon-pricing feasibility screen, simplified versions of three IMF and World Bank macro-fiscal models and a debt sustainability test in one workbook for 186 countries. It takes the same reproducibility standard as the tools here, but it extends CPAT, so it is presented with the modular upgrades in section 6. Its Kenya run finds a net zero budget need of 0.5 percent of GDP in 2030, of which feasible power-sector carbon pricing covers about 5 percent (illustrative tool results, not forecasts).

# A one-page fiscal profile from public data (paper 7.2) {.unnumbered}

Before advising on carbon pricing, subsidy reform or climate investment, an analyst needs a quick, comparable view of a country's fiscal space, spending capacity, cost of capital and fossil fuel exposure. The Global Fiscal Indicators dashboard assembles 80 indicators in twelve blocks for 217 economies from about twenty public datasets, scores them on one 1-to-10 scale and shows a one-page profile. A scripted pipeline rebuilds everything from the raw files, never imputes, records the year and source of every value, and stops if its configuration and outputs disagree. A comparison of four middle-income economies shows how the profile separates a revenue problem from a debt-service problem.

# How the tools connect {.unnumbered}

The tools feed the rest of the program. The excise diagnostic can supply checked starting tax rates and externality values for CPAT (section 5) and for the carbon-pricing papers (section 1). The scenario tool's investment needs and debt test (paper 6.5) carry the cost-of-capital argument of section 3 into a country's budget. The dashboard tells an analyst which of these lenses matters most for a given country before any model is run.
